data.content_ref: inline:{"analogy":null,"claim":"Ownership-based allocation is a greedy optimization strategy that is locally efficient but globally suboptimal. It does not systematically suppress cross-cutting explanations but merely defers their discovery until the marginal efficiency of within-lineage search drops below the cost of cross-lineage transfer.","counterconditions":[{"case":"The cost of cross-lineage transfer is infinite or unbounded (e.g., incommensurability), so the deferral never terminates.","eval":"observation"},{"case":"The system terminates before the saturation point is reached, so the deferral becomes permanent suppression.","eval":"observation"},{"case":"Within-lineage search is non-saturating (infinitely productive), so the cross-over point is never reached.","eval":"observation"}],"definitions":[],"derivation":[],"formalization_refs":[],"mechanism":"The cost of formulating a cross-cutting explanation includes the cost of acquiring a rival's vocabulary and the risk of incompatibility. In the early stages of problem-solving, within-lineage search has a low marginal cost because the vocabulary and commitments are already loaded. Ownership allocation greedily exploits this low cost. As the within-lineage search saturates (all local moves exhausted), the marginal cost of further within-lineage work rises. Eventually, this cost exceeds the fixed cost of cross-lineage transfer, at which point a cross-cutting explanation becomes economically rational. Thus, the apparent 'suppression' is just a rational deferral under a cost-of-search model.","premises":[],"schema":"deepreason-reasoning-envelope-v1","scope":{"covers":[],"excludes":[]},"simulation_refs":[],"uncertainties":[]}
